items.summary:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most intelligent and aligned AI model to date, designed to excel in computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional tasks. Astra achieves top scores on multiple benchmarks, including FrontierMath Tier 4 and ARC-AGI-3, and is being made available to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS.

GPT-6 Astra offers significant improvements in speed, accuracy, and safety for computer-based tasks such as online research, data analysis, software installation, and website creation. It also enhances professional workflows by producing well-structured documents, presentations, and spreadsheets that adhere to user templates and styles. The model demonstrates better judgment in ambiguous situations and reduces token usage compared to previous versions, aiming to increase efficiency and output quality across various domains.

items.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra achieves state-of-the-art scores on ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, surpassing human action efficiency with novel symbolic modeling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on ARC-AGI-3
items.summary:
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra scored 62.7% and 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark using two different harnesses, outperforming the human baseline in action efficiency on 96% of levels. The model demonstrated the ability to convert unfamiliar environments into compact symbolic world models, developing a custom domain-specific language to track state and plan actions effectively.

ARC-AGI-3 is a benchmark designed to evaluate agentic intelligence through abstract, turn-based environments that require exploration, modeling, goal-setting, and planning without explicit instructions. Astra's performance represents a significant advancement in measuring artificial general intelligence capabilities, with its efficient reasoning reducing the cost of solving tasks compared to human participants.

Analysis of Astra's behavior revealed its use of a compact algebraic notation to represent game mechanics and multi-step plans, enabling precise and information-dense internal models. This approach allowed Astra to build custom tools and strategies on the fly, highlighting progress toward AI systems that can acquire and apply skills as efficiently as humans.

items.title: Analysis of 17,000 runs reveals tool choices by coding agents Claude, Codex, and Cursor across 75 simulated repositories in 10 languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Which tools do Claude, Codex and Cursor choose? We measured 17k runs to find out
items.summary:
Researchers conducted 16,893 experiments using coding agents Claude, Codex, and Cursor on 75 simulated GitHub repositories representing various programming languages and sectors. They used a simulated human-in-the-loop approach and multiple sandbox environments to evaluate how these agents select third-party tools and implement solutions for real-world coding tasks.

The study found that Codex relies heavily on focused web searches, Cursor uses web sources in about two-thirds of cases, and Claude primarily depends on its internal knowledge but browses more pages when it searches. The experiments aimed to reflect realistic developer scenarios and revealed differing strategies among agents in tool selection and implementation.

items.title: IFM releases K2 Horizon, a connected fleet of six open AI models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters with state-of-the-art performance and full training lifecycle transparency [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: K2 Horizon: A connected fleet of six open models
items.summary:
IFM has launched K2 Horizon, a fleet of six AI models spanning from 0.9 billion to 375 billion parameters, delivering top-tier performance in reasoning, mathematics, coding, and agentic tasks across various deployment environments from edge devices to enterprise. The release includes comprehensive open access to training data, intermediate checkpoints, code, configurations, and evaluation results under Apache 2.0 and applicable dataset licenses, enabling researchers and developers to study and reproduce the full training lifecycle including agentic post-training.

The fleet features models optimized for different scales, with smaller models designed for constrained devices like watches and phones, and larger models for local workstations and enterprise use. The 36B-A4B model introduces a Mixture-of-Value-Attention mechanism that enhances efficiency, while the 0.9B, 3.7B, and 7B models set new state-of-the-art benchmarks in their size classes. K2 Horizon's unified architecture and tooling facilitate dynamic routing and capability studies across scales, marking it as the most comprehensive open model release to date.

items.title: Developer ports 1993 Amiga game Babylonian Twins to Godot using a large language model to read 68000 assembly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Porting my 1993 Amiga game to Godot, with an LLM reading the 68000 assembly
items.summary:
A developer has ported the 1993 Amiga game Babylonian Twins to the Godot engine by leveraging a large language model (LLM) to interpret the original 68000 assembly code. The original game was built on an Amiga 500 with direct hardware programming in assembly, created under challenging conditions in Baghdad during sanctions. The LLM automated the reading and conversion of the assembly code, speeding up the porting process compared to previous manual efforts.

The project involved running the LLM in an environment with access to the original toolchain and filesystem, allowing it to assemble, build, and test the game autonomously. The port includes features such as command-line flags for automated testing and level loading. This approach demonstrated the LLM's ability to understand and translate low-level, undocumented code from a discontinued platform, enabling the original game to run within a modern engine.

items.title: New York City Mayor Mamdani imposes one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in schools through 8th grade starting 2026-27 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: NYC mayor Mamdani imposes 1 year ban on AI for schools through 8th grade
items.summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels announced a one-year moratorium on the use of student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in public schools from pre-kindergarten through 8th grade, affecting nearly 600,000 students. The policy aims to prioritize human instruction and student safety while studying AI's impact on education before considering future integration.

items.title: Study finds 35% of new websites by mid-2025 contain AI-generated or AI-assisted text, with increased semantic similarity but no clear drop in factual accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Impact of AI-Generated Text on the Internet
items.summary:
Researchers from Imperial College London, Internet Archive, and Stanford University analyzed a representative sample of websites from 2022 to 2025 to assess the prevalence and impact of AI-generated text on the internet. They found that by mid-2025, about 35% of newly published websites were AI-generated or AI-assisted, a rise from zero before ChatGPT's launch in late 2022. The study observed increased semantic similarity and positive sentiment in AI-generated content but did not find statistically significant evidence of decreased factual accuracy or stylistic diversity.

The team used multiple AI detection methods and surveyed US adults about their perceptions of AI's impact, revealing a divergence between public concerns and measured effects. Their findings suggest that while AI-generated text is becoming widespread and influencing online discourse, some feared negative impacts like truth decay are not yet supported by data.

items.title: Mistral launches Agentic Search to improve AI-driven document navigation and retrieval with higher accuracy and lower latency [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic Search
items.summary:
Mistral has introduced Agentic Search, a retrieval layer designed to enhance AI systems' ability to navigate, read, and verify information within complex documents. The technology supports sensitive domain-specific data and integrates with existing search indexes to deliver more accurate results while reducing latency and token usage, as demonstrated by significant improvements on FinanceBench and OfficeQA Pro benchmarks.

Agentic Search addresses limitations of traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by enabling multi-step retrieval loops that allow AI models to iteratively search, inspect, and verify information across multiple sources. This approach helps enterprises unlock value from proprietary and confidential data stored behind isolation boundaries, improving AI performance on dense, multi-document queries that require reasoning beyond single-pass retrieval.

items.title: Pew Research finds 10% of English-language webpages show AI authorship signs in 2026, rising to over one-third for pages published after ChatGPT's 2022 release [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much of the Internet Is Written with AI?
items.summary:
Pew Research analyzed nearly half a million English-language webpages from the past five years using AI detection tools and found that 10% of pages in a July 2026 sample showed significant signs of AI authorship. This share rises to over one-third when considering only pages published after ChatGPT's release in late 2022, reflecting a growing trend in AI-generated or AI-edited online content.

The study also found that AI-authored text is unevenly distributed across web domains, with about 10% of .com pages showing AI signs compared to lower rates on .org, .edu, and .gov domains. Linguistic patterns such as frequent use of em dashes, Oxford commas, and certain vocabulary terms were identified as common features of AI-generated writing. These findings highlight the increasing presence of AI in shaping internet content and raise questions about authenticity and trust online.

This share rises to over one-third when considering only pages published after ChatGPT's release in late 2022, reflecting a growing trend in AI-generated or AI-edited online content.

The study also found that AI-authored text is unevenly distributed across web domains, with about 10% of .com pages showing AI signs compared to lower rates on .org, .edu, and .gov domains. Linguistic patterns such as frequent use of em dashes, Oxford commas, and certain vocabulary terms were identified as common features of AI-generated writing. These findings highlight the increasing presence of AI in shaping internet content and raise questions about authenticity and trust online.

Google DeepMind has introduced WeatherNext 3, its most advanced AI weather forecasting model that uses real-time satellite data to deliver hourly, high-resolution predictions globally. The model offers forecasts five times sharper than its predecessor, improving accuracy for temperature, precipitation, and wind patterns. WeatherNext 3 is integrated across Google Search, Maps, Gemini, and Google Cloud, enhancing weather information accessibility for users and developers.

Unlike traditional physics-based simulations with data lags, WeatherNext 3 learns directly from live satellite observations, enabling rapid updates and precise local forecasts at resolutions as fine as 5 kilometers. This advancement supports better planning in agriculture, renewable energy, and daily activities by providing timely and detailed weather insights worldwide.

items.title: Pangram emerges as leading AI text detection tool amid debate over its reliability and impact on publishing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pangram Has Emerged as the Gold Standard of AI Detection. Should You Trust It?
items.summary:
Pangram, a Brooklyn-based AI startup, has gained prominence as a top tool for detecting AI-generated text, claiming to estimate the percentage of AI involvement in writing. The company has been involved in high-profile cases where its detection influenced publishing decisions, including the cancellation of a novel's release and scrutiny of major publications. Founded in 2023 by former Google and Tesla employees, Pangram uses techniques like synthetic mirroring and hard negative mining to train its models, serving industries such as education and legal sectors.

Despite its growing adoption, Pangram faces skepticism from some writers and experts who question the trustworthiness and fairness of AI detection software. The company emphasizes its use of properly licensed datasets and aims to address concerns about AI's impact on creative fields, but debates continue over the accuracy and consequences of labeling content as AI-generated. Pangram's role in the evolving landscape of AI content detection highlights ongoing tensions between technological innovation and creative integrity.

items.title: Multiplayer AI Manifesto proposes principles for collaborative AI agents to reduce context loss and improve productivity across enterprise workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Multiplayer AI Manifesto
items.summary:
The Multiplayer AI Manifesto outlines five principles aimed at enabling AI systems to operate collaboratively across multiple users and tools, addressing the limitations of siloed AI chats. It emphasizes open, shared agent sessions that integrate with existing work platforms to reduce context switching and improve organizational learning and security.

The manifesto highlights challenges such as the "context tax" caused by isolated AI interactions and the risks of AI agents acting without enterprise-wide security controls. It cites studies and examples, including a Harvard Business School experiment and Shopify's internal AI system, to demonstrate the productivity gains from multiplayer AI. The manifesto calls for AI agents to continuously improve, share knowledge, and automate routine communication to allow humans to focus on higher-value tasks.

items.title: Epoch.ai launches FrontierMath Erdős benchmark to rigorously evaluate AI on selected unsolved Erdős math problems using formal verification and open-source tools [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FrontierMath Erdős
items.summary:
Epoch.ai has introduced FrontierMath Erdős, a new benchmark designed to measure AI capabilities in solving selected unsolved math problems posed by Paul Erdős. The benchmark focuses on 68 problems curated for their mathematical significance and difficulty, aiming to provide a more rigorous and transparent evaluation framework for AI math performance.

The initiative addresses challenges in curation, verification, and replicability by collaborating with mathematician Thomas Bloom for problem selection, using the Lean proof assistant for formal verification of AI-generated solutions, and open-sourcing the entire benchmark codebase. This approach seeks to improve transparency and reliability in tracking AI progress on complex mathematical problems.

Nvidia has introduced the Personal AI Router (PAIR), a software solution that connects compatible Windows, macOS, and Linux systems with NVIDIA RTX GPUs and DGX Spark systems into a personal AI cluster. PAIR enables these devices to share local AI inference workloads across the network while keeping data private and on-premises.

PAIR supports routing AI tasks across multiple devices without requiring special hardware setups, allowing users to maximize local compute resources for AI applications and agents. It integrates with existing local inference backends like Ollama and LM Studio and operates without sending prompts or files to the cloud, preserving user privacy.

items.originalTitle: Inside Meta’s Efforts to Ensure Its Upcoming ‘Hatch’ AI Agent Won’t Go Rogue
items.summary:
Meta Platforms is preparing to launch Hatch, a new personal AI agent designed to assist users with tasks ranging from health to finances. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has emphasized the importance of ensuring the agent's safety and reliability before release.

The company has conducted extensive internal testing, known as dogfooding, to identify and fix undesirable behaviors in Hatch. These efforts aim to enable the agent to act effectively on users' behalf while minimizing costly mistakes, with the launch expected in the coming weeks.

items.originalSummary:
Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said AI agents will soon be able to help with everything from health to relationships to finances. First, the company needs to make them safe.

That’s been the focus of an extensive effort as Meta prepares to release what it hopes to be a landmark new personal agent called Hatch in the coming weeks. Months of testing by its own employees—a process known as dogfooding—has turned up a range of undesirable behaviors by Hatch that the company has worked to fix as it tries to ensure the service has the capability and access to act effectively on users’ behalf without straying into costly mistakes.

The platform, originally available for MacOS and Windows, has now expanded its accessibility by launching dedicated iOS applications, allowing users to engage with their projects on Apple mobile devices.

Crew operates locally without requiring accounts or servers, supporting shared or local workspaces and enabling users to connect multiple AI agents through their own CLI accounts. The platform includes features like multi-agent threads, ticket boards for project planning, token usage tracking, and integrated tools such as file explorers, terminals, and synchronized music playback to enhance collaborative workflows.

items.title: Snowflake reports 28% growth in CoCo coding assistant users as enterprises seek AI tools beyond Anthropic models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Snowflake Results Show Enterprises’ Desire For Anthropic Buffer
items.summary: Snowflake's latest quarterly report highlights growing enterprise demand for AI coding tools that integrate multiple models rather than relying solely on Anthropic. The company's CoCo coding assistant, which uses Anthropic and OpenAI models, saw a 28% increase in customer accounts in the July quarter, reaching 9,100 accounts. Snowflake is also expanding CoCo's capabilities by adding open-weight and open-source models like DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3 to offer more cost-effective and flexible AI solutions for corporate CIOs.

Snowflake is also expanding CoCo's capabilities by adding open-weight and open-source models like DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3 to offer more cost-effective and flexible AI solutions for corporate CIOs.
items.originalSummary:
Snowflake’s strong quarterly report on Wednesday said a lot about what can go right for older software firms that sell AI tools on top of their existing products. 

While Anthropic, OpenAI and Cursor get the lion’s share of headlines about AI coding, for instance, Snowflake, whose primary business is selling data management software, demonstrated in its earnings that there’s a much longer list of firms that can provide such products. That’s in part because corporate chief information officers are looking for cost-savings after a fast run-up of AI spending earlier in the year, and they may want coding tools that can access a multitude of models rather than getting locked into one controlled by a single model maker like Anthropic.

Snowflake said Wednesday that the number of customer accounts using CoCo, its coding assistant previously known as Cortex Code, grew at least 28% in the July quarter to 9,100, compared to the previous period. (Enterprises may have multiple accounts for different teams within their firms). CoCo currently relies on models from Anthropic and OpenAI but is adding open-weight and open-source source models such as DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3, a spokesperson said.

items.originalTitle: What Anthropic's IPO Investors Want to Know
items.summary:
Anthropic is set to release its initial public offering prospectus after Labor Day, marking the first time public investors will see a comprehensive financial overview of the AI company behind Claude. While private investors have had access to growth and revenue projections, public investors are seeking more detailed information beyond standard financial statements.

Executives at Anthropic have engaged in discussions with potential large investors about providing additional AI-related business metrics, such as AI tokenomics, revenue per gigawatt of compute, and net revenue retention rates. However, it remains uncertain whether the company will disclose these specific performance indicators in its IPO filings.

items.originalSummary:
We’re getting ready for Anthropic to make its initial public offering prospectus public sometime after Labor Day. Though the company’s private investors have had a window into its torrid growth and projections, this will be the first time public investors are getting a full financial picture of the Claude maker. 

Just how complete a picture remains a big question, though. We’re hearing that investors want a lot more from Anthropic than the financial statements that securities regulators generally require companies to report. 

In a series of meetings, executives at Anthropic have been going back and forth with potential large investors on whether the company can provide other business- or performance-related metrics particular to AI. These include AI tokenomics, including what it makes off every AI token it processes, how much revenue it’s generating per gigawatt of compute, and net revenue retention, a measure of a tech vendor’s ability to keep customers and increase their spending. There’s no guarantee Anthropic will provide any of these.

items.title: Abliteration.ai offers commercial access to open-weight AI models with removed guardrails for offensive cybersecurity and red-teaming tasks [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Abliteration.ai is making a business out of removing AI guardrails
items.summary:
Abliteration.ai has launched a service providing access to powerful open-weight AI models stripped of safety guardrails, including Z.ai's GLM-5.3, to support offensive cybersecurity, red-teaming, and agent testing. The startup hosts these modified models via web and API, aiming to enable defenders to replicate harmful behaviors for improved security, though the removal of safeguards also facilitates potentially dangerous uses.

The company, founded in late 2025 and incorporated in March 2026, operates without venture capital funding but has deals with major cloud providers and offers a moderation layer for customers to add guardrails. Critics warn that abliterated models could be misused for harm, with experts suggesting government intervention through content classifiers and customer identity verification. Abliteration.ai acknowledges the challenge of balancing access and responsibility as it develops further safety measures.

items.title: OpenAI commits $1 billion to Daybreak initiative providing AI cyber defense tools and training for frontline defenders of essential services [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Daybreak for Frontline Defenders: $1B to protect essential services
items.summary:
OpenAI has launched Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, a $1 billion global initiative to expand subsidized access to advanced AI cyber defense models, training, and technical support for organizations protecting essential services such as water, electricity, local government, and banking. The program prioritizes resource-constrained defenders in the United States and plans to extend support internationally through partnerships and the Daybreak Defense Network.

The initiative addresses the growing threat of AI-enabled cyber attacks by equipping defenders with tools to identify vulnerabilities, analyze suspicious activity, and develop fixes before attackers exploit weaknesses. OpenAI's commitment includes a pilot with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center and aims to help defenders manage complex and aging infrastructure systems with limited budgets and expertise.

items.title: OpenAI launches Astra, its most powerful AI model with advanced cybersecurity and coding capabilities, available to Daybreak and paid plan users [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI launches Astra, its powerful (and controversial) new model
items.summary:
OpenAI introduced Astra, its latest AI model, claiming it offers unmatched speed, accuracy, and safety for computer and browser tasks. The model is initially available to Daybreak cybersecurity customers and will roll out to other paid plans and API users over the following week. OpenAI president Greg Brockman described Astra as the company's most intelligent and aligned model, representing a significant advancement in AI delegation and empowerment.

Astra features enhanced cybersecurity abilities, including identifying zero-day exploits to aid defenders, and excels in software engineering benchmarks compared to previous models. However, Astra's use of opaque recurrence, which obscures the chain of thought monitoring process, has sparked controversy. OpenAI acknowledges the challenge of monitoring more capable models and frames some opacity as a natural evolution. While Astra's release prompted questions about artificial general intelligence (AGI), OpenAI clarified that AGI is no longer a contractual milestone but a conceptual idea, leaving its classification open to interpretation.

items.summary:
OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, and xAI's Grok all faced outages on the morning of September 3, disrupting their AI chatbot services. While xAI attributed its Grok outage to a compute center issue in Memphis, OpenAI cited a routing error, and Anthropic did not disclose specific causes.

The outages coincided but were not linked to a shared third-party provider, as major cloud and internet infrastructure companies reported no issues. OpenAI and Anthropic have not confirmed any common source for the disruptions, and xAI apologized to affected compute partners amid its ongoing partnership with Anthropic and SpaceX.

items.title: Researchers identify interpretable symptom vectors for depression in a large language model, aligning internal activations with clinical assessments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpretable Symptom Vectors for Depression in a Large Language Model
items.summary: Researchers analyzed the internal activations of the Gemma-3-27B-PT large language model to understand how depressive symptoms are represented, finding that symptom groups separate distinctly at a specific model layer. They used mechanistic interpretability techniques and Semantic Projection to map naturalistic text onto symptom vectors derived from validated clinical instruments, preserving clinician-annotated symptom rankings across mood, somatic, and suicidality dimensions. A single depression vector at layer 21 effectively distinguishes depressive from non-depressive text, suggesting potential for interpretable depression-assessment tools based on model activations.

They used mechanistic interpretability techniques and Semantic Projection to map naturalistic text onto symptom vectors derived from validated clinical instruments, preserving clinician-annotated symptom rankings across mood, somatic, and suicidality dimensions. A single depression vector at layer 21 effectively distinguishes depressive from non-depressive text, suggesting potential for interpretable depression-assessment tools based on model activations.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.01832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Patients with depression present with diverse symptom profiles, yet clinical practice routinely reduces this variation to a single severity score. Large language models (LLMs) can potentially capture various symptoms and their severity from patient speech. However, how depressive symptoms are represented inside LLMs remains poorly understood, limiting clinical trust. To examine whether internal model activations match clinician judgment, we analyzed the residual stream of Gemma-3-27B-PT using mechanistic interpretability techniques. Recording activations across symptom descriptions drawn from validated clinical instruments, we found that symptom groups geometrically separated the most at layer 21 across multiple distance metrics. Using Semantic Projection, we then projected held-out naturalistic text onto Symptom Vectors constructed from these instruments. The resulting per-symptom coefficients preserved clinician-annotated rank ordering across mood, somatic, and suicidality axes. Furthermore, a single depression vector in Layer 21 separates held-out depressive from non-depressive text (AUC = 0.789), which can be used as an emotional valence gate that restricts symptom projection to depressive speech. These results reveal a decorrelated, clinician-aligned symptom signal readable directly from internal activations, offering a mechanistic foundation for interpretable depression-assessment tools.

items.title: Researchers introduce Sparse Readout Prism to explain logit-lens scores via sparse readout features independent of corpus fitting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse Readout Prism: Explaining Logit-Lens Scores in Features Instead of Tokens
items.summary: Researchers present Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), a method that decomposes the readout matrix of language models into sparse features to explain logit-lens scores without relying on corpus fitting. SRP reveals stable readout features that provide a new unit of analysis beyond token identities and reconstructs more logit differences than existing baselines. This approach addresses corpus conditionality by offering a corpus-independent control for analyzing intermediate hidden states in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.01936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model's prediction of its next token develops across layers, and lens methods track this process by decoding intermediate hidden states into tokens. But a lens reading reflects both the hidden state and the readout (the unembedding matrix) used to decode it. Many lenses are fit on a corpus, and we show that two lenses differing only in their fitting corpus can report different tokens for the same hidden states. We call this dependence corpus conditionality. To examine readout structure independently of the fitting corpus, we introduce Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), which decomposes the readout using only its weights and expresses any token logit or logit difference as a sum of contributions from sparse readout features. This reveals readout features as a new unit of analysis for lens readings, exposing structure that token identities can obscure and enabling comparisons across tokens, contexts, layers, and lenses. Replacing the original readout with SRP's sparse approximation reconstructs 8.9-17.3 percentage points more of the tested logit differences than the strongest of six baselines built on geometric relations among readout rows. Ablating features shifts logit differences in proportion to their SRP contributions. Although token readings vary with the fitting corpus, the dominant readout feature remains stable. Because SRP uses no corpus in its construction, it provides a control independent of the fitting corpus for lens analyses.

items.title: Study finds large language models generate less diverse outputs than their training data across multiple model families and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Large Language Models Capture the Diversity in their Training Data?
items.summary: Researchers analyzed large language models including OLMo, Pythia, and GPT-Neo to compare the conditional entropy of their outputs with that of their training data, revealing that model-generated outputs consistently exhibit lower diversity. This conditional diversity gap was also observed in other generative models such as class-conditioned ImageNet generators and text-conditioned models trained on MS-COCO. To address this, the study proposes a post-hoc correction method that generates multiple outputs per input and reweights them using a matrix-entropy projection, increasing output diversity while staying close to the original model distribution. The researchers provide an information-theoretic framework and a scalable algorithm to measure and mitigate this diversity gap in generative models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are trained to model conditional distributions over text, yet it remains inadequately understood whether they capture the full diversity of plausible outputs present in their training data. We study this question through an information-theoretic lens by comparing the conditional entropy of model-generated outputs with that of the corresponding training data. Given paired input-output samples, we use conditional entropy and its matrix-based analogue based on von Neumann entropy to measure output variability beyond what is explained by the conditioning input, without requiring multiple reference outputs for the same prompt. Across LLM families with publicly available training data, including OLMo, Pythia, and GPT-Neo, we consistently find that model-generated outputs exhibit lower conditional entropy than their training data, across different model scales, sequence lengths, and decoding strategies. We observe a similar conditional diversity gap beyond language modeling, including class-conditioned ImageNet generators and text-conditioned models trained on MS-COCO. To address this gap, we propose a post-hoc correction mechanism that generates multiple outputs for each input and reweights them through a matrix-entropy projection, increasing conditional diversity while remaining close to the original model distribution. We prove the concavity of the matrix-based conditional entropy functional, which makes the resulting entropy-constrained projection a convex optimization problem, and develop a scalable mirror-descent algorithm for its implementation. Our results reveal a systematic conditional diversity gap between modern generative models and their training data, and provide an information-theoretic framework for measuring and mitigating this gap.

items.title: Researchers propose TaRA method to improve Low-Rank Adaptation initialization by aligning low-rank gradients with full-rank model gradients for better fine-tuning performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TaRA: Training-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization
items.summary: Researchers introduce Training-aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization (TaRA), a method designed to enhance Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by initializing it so that gradients from low-rank factors closely match those of the full-rank weight matrix. This approach addresses sensitivity in LoRA performance caused by initialization and the information bottleneck from low-rank decomposition. TaRA is derived from a mathematical formulation and adds minimal computational overhead. Across various fine-tuning tasks, TaRA consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art initialization methods, offering a simple, robust, and scalable solution for effective LoRA initialization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a de facto standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet its performance is highly sensitive to initialization due to the information bottleneck imposed by low-rank decomposition. Existing approaches attempt to construct high-quality LoRA initializations by exploiting principal components of pretrained weights, activations, or gradients. However, these methods do not directly account for the training dynamics of the full-rank model. In this paper, we propose Training-aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization (TaRA), a method that initializes LoRA such that the gradients induced by the low-rank factors closely approximate the gradient of the corresponding full-rank weight matrix. Derived from a mathematical formulation, TaRA improves gradient fidelity at the start of training while introducing negligible computational overhead. Across diverse and challenging fine-tuning tasks, TaRA consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, establishing a simple, robust, and scalable solution for effective LoRA initialization.

items.title: Researchers introduce Declarative Attention protocol enabling language models to control their own attention, reducing token processing by up to 52% with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention
items.summary: Researchers propose Declarative Attention (DA), a new protocol that allows language models to declare which parts of the context to attend to during generation, partitioning attention into global, focus, and local modes. This approach reduces the need to read the entire key-value cache, significantly cutting the number of tokens processed during decoding. Evaluated zero-shot on 15 long-context tasks using off-the-shelf models like Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-27B, DA reduced total attended tokens by 52.0% and 31.1% respectively, with modest accuracy drops that decrease as model size increases. DA introduces a new form of sparse attention with potential for further improvements through training-based methods in future research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models spend most of their attention on a small fraction of context, yet they read the entire KV cache to find the few tokens that matter. If the user asks about a previous detail in a 1M-token conversation, global attention layers must scan the full context to generate each token of the reply. A prominent approach mitigates this cost by pre-selecting relevant tokens via lightweight proxy scores, but this extrinsic scoring still incurs O(N) per step. We take an intrinsic approach motivated by the simple question: wouldn't the model already know which parts of the context are relevant? To this end, we introduce Declarative Attention (DA), a protocol that elicits the model to declare where it needs to attend within its chain-of-thought, partitioning generation into three modes: <global> (full context), <focus> (a specific region), and <local> (recent output only). The inference engine parses these declarations like tool calls and skips most of the KV cache read. Under zero-shot evaluation across 15 long-context tasks, DA on off-the-shelf models (Gemma-4-31B, Qwen-3.6-27B) significantly reduces total attended tokens during decoding (52.0%, 31.1%) with modest accuracy drops (1.27pp, 2.75pp) that shrink with model scale. DA unlocks a new axis of sparse attention, with further potential under training-based methods that future work can explore.

items.title: Researchers analyze how misleading context corrupts medical question answering in large language models, testing fabricated evidence and assertions on 8,627 MedMisBench questions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Untangling the Mechanisms of Misleading Context in Medical Question Answering
items.summary: Researchers studied how misleading context affects large language models' medical question answering by injecting fabricated evidence and bare assertions into 8,627 clinician-reviewed questions from MedMisBench. They tested three reasoning models, finding all were more susceptible to assertions than fabricated evidence, with misleading cues disclosed more often in reasoning traces than in final responses. The study revealed that fabricated evidence corrupts reasoning early and accumulates, while assertions redirect conclusions near the end. An open model's reasoning trace allowed a monitoring system to detect 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives, outperforming detection from responses alone. The findings highlight that the most misleading contexts are disclosed least and are detectable mainly through open reasoning traces, which are often withheld by frontier providers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models now answer medical questions with expert-level performance. However, the context these systems act on can be misleading, and misleading context can corrupt a model's medical judgment. To understand how misleading context corrupts this judgment, we examine the model's susceptibility to the context, disclosure of it, mechanism of corrupted reasoning, and monitorability of the decision. On the medical reasoning subset of MedMisBench, a clinician-reviewed question-answering benchmark of 8,627 questions, we inject two types of misleading context cues, fabricated evidence and a bare assertion. We test three reasoning models, two that expose their full reasoning trace and one frontier model that exposes only its response. All three are more susceptible to the assertion than to the fabricated evidence, adopting the asserted answer 10 to 27 points more often. The misleading cues are disclosed in 81 to 98% of traces but only 7 to 90% of responses, and the assertion is disclosed less often than evidence based cues. Resampling from reasoning traces without disclosure shows the two cues corrupt reasoning differently, evidence entering early and accumulating while the assertion redirects the conclusion near its end. An LLM monitor catches 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives when reading an open model's trace with guidance, against at most 32% from any response. The misleading context that models are most susceptible to is disclosed least, and was caught reliably only from an open reasoning trace, which frontier providers withhold.

items.title: Researchers introduce influence-guided response rewriting to enhance training data attribution effects in large language models, showing stronger behavioral shifts than traditional reweighting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Reweighting to Rewriting: Unlocking the Intervention Effects of Influential Samples in Training Data Attribution
items.summary: Training data attribution (TDA) seeks to identify which training examples influence model behavior, but its effectiveness depends on both the examples chosen and how they are modified. Researchers found that influence functions (IF), which estimate changes under small reweighting, often yield limited impact when used for reweighting interventions. To address this, they propose influence-guided response rewriting, replacing responses of influential examples with behavior-aligned or opposed supervision while keeping instructions fixed. This method was tested across four open-weight large language models using epistemic abstention as a benchmark, producing stronger, more persistent, and bidirectional behavioral changes compared to reweighting the same examples.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) aims to identify training examples that shape model behavior, but its intervention value depends on both which examples are selected and how they are modified. Influence functions (IF) estimate behavioral changes under infinitesimal reweighting, yet IF-selected examples often show limited advantages over random selection under conventional weight-based interventions. This raises the question of whether influential examples lack intervention value or whether reweighting fails to realize their behavioral leverage.We introduce influence-guided response rewriting, which uses IF to identify intervention targets and replaces their responses with behavior-aligned or behavior-opposed supervision while keeping instructions fixed. Across four open-weight LLMs, we compare rewriting and reweighting on the same influence-selected examples using epistemic abstention as our primary testbed. Response rewriting produces stronger, more persistent, and bidirectional behavioral shifts, while reweighting the same examples yields weak and inconsistent effects. Further analyses show that influence-selected examples provide greater rewriting leverage than alternative selectors, with changes remaining concentrated on target-relevant behaviors. The same qualitative contrast extends to safety refusal. These results distinguish the local reweighting effects captured by influence estimates from the broader intervention leverage of the examples they identify, motivating intervention-aware evaluation of TDA methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.01736v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with external tools have demonstrated remarkable capability in solving complex real-world tasks. However, existing approaches suffer from two key challenges: brittle multi-step and multi-turn reasoning caused by incompatible tool output types and API schemas, and performance degradation under large tool catalogues. items.title: Researchers present two techniques to improve realism in AI alignment evaluations by using inference-time compute and deployment-like agent harnesses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
items.summary: Researchers address the challenge of evaluation awareness in AI alignment by introducing two methods that make simulated evaluations more similar to real deployments. The first method, critique refinement, uses additional inference-time compute to generate and refine multiple candidate actions for more realistic simulation. The second method, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target model in an agent harness to better mimic real deployment environments in coding tasks. Testing on multiple models shows that combining both techniques yields greater realism improvements than using either alone. These automated approaches enhance the effectiveness of alignment evaluations by using extra compute more efficiently than simply extending audit duration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that they compose: applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. Our results show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that these improvements use additional compute more effectively than making the audits longer.

items.title: Researchers propose scalable Kronecker-Fisher approximation for efficient Hessian analysis in billion-parameter language models, revealing key vulnerability patterns and aiding compression strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Scalable Kronecker-Fisher Approximation: Efficient Hessian Analysis for Billion-Parameter Language Models Compression
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a scalable Kronecker-based approximation method that enables practical Hessian analysis of billion-parameter language models without storing the full Fisher matrix. This approach identifies consistent vulnerability patterns, notably high sensitivity and strong cross-layer correlations in value projection layers across multiple model families, while other components show architecture-specific behaviors.

The team conducted extensive experiments involving quantization, sparsification, inter-layer corruption, and fine-tuning after corruption, demonstrating that their approximation correlates strongly with both performance degradation and recovery. This framework offers a theoretically grounded tool for pinpointing fragile components in large models, facilitating guided compression and optimization techniques such as mixed-precision allocation, layer-wise sparsity, and adaptive low-rank decomposition at both layer and weight group levels.

Our approach reveals consistent vulnerability patterns: value projection layers exhibit the highest sensitivity and strongest cross-layer correlations across multiple model families, while other components exhibit architecture-specific behaviors. Through extensive experiments on quantization, sparsification, inter-layer corruption, and post-corruption fine-tuning, we demonstrate that our approximation strongly correlates with both performance degradation and recovery. Our framework provides a practical, theoretically grounded tool for identifying fragile components in large models, opening new avenues for guided compression and optimization strategies, such as mixed-precision allocation, layer-wise sparsity, and adaptive low-rank decomposition across layers and even individual weight groups.

items.title: Loom introduces embedding-space reweighting to aggregate free-text diagnostic hypotheses for root cause analysis, achieving faster inference with competitive accuracy on OpenRCA benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Loom: Weaving Diagnostic Strands into Free-Text Consensus via Embedding-Space Reweighting
items.summary:
Loom is a generative consensus framework designed to combine noisy and conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus for root cause analysis (RCA) in industrial NLP applications. It projects modular heuristic-generated hypotheses into a continuous embedding space and uses an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm to resolve conflicts, followed by a single lightweight large language model (LLM) synthesis step. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark, Loom matches or closely trails state-of-the-art autonomous agents across multiple datasets while significantly reducing inference latency by approximately 26 to 33 times compared to heavier LLM synthesizers.

The framework bridges the gap between traditional weak supervision methods, which are limited to discrete classes, and monolithic LLM agents that face context and latency challenges. Deployment experiences highlight trade-offs between agentic depth and inference speed, challenges in redundancy detection, and the benefits of deterministic consensus in building trust among subject matter experts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aggregating noisy, conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus is a fundamental challenge when deploying NLP systems in real-world industrial settings. While monolithic Large Language Model (LLM) agents offer unbounded expressivity for tasks like Root Cause Analysis (RCA), they suffer from context limits, compounding hallucinations, and prohibitive inference latency. Traditional weak supervision offers statistical rigor but is mathematically restricted to discrete classes. We present Loom, a generative consensus framework deployed for real-world RCA that bridges these paradigms. Loom aggregates open-form hypotheses emitted by modular heuristics (diagnostic templates dynamically populated with episode-specific entities, times, and metrics) by projecting them into a continuous embedding space, and resolves conflicting signals with an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm. The resulting consensus weights ground a single lightweight LLM synthesis step. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark, Loom occupies the accuracy--efficiency Pareto frontier: it matches a state-of-the-art autonomous agent on Bank and Market-2 and trails on Market-1 and Telecom, while using a single LLM call per incident on all four datasets ($\sim$26$\times$ faster; $\sim$33$\times$ with an 8B-parameter synthesizer). We discuss our deployment experience, highlighting lessons learned regarding the trade-offs between agentic depth and inference latency, negative results in redundancy detection, and how deterministic consensus fosters trust among Subject Matter Experts~(SMEs).

items.title: Researchers find substantial incoherence in language model probabilistic forecasts using Dutch-book analysis on stock return events [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dutch Books for Language Models
items.summary: Researchers evaluated the coherence of probabilistic forecasts generated by language models using a method based on de Finetti's theorem and Dutch-book analysis, which measures the guaranteed profit an arbitrageur could make betting against the model's probabilities. They applied this method to forecasts on events derived from stock returns data without requiring outcome labels, allowing assessment even when outcomes are unresolved. The study found significant incoherence in language model forecasts, which worsened with more complex logical relationships between events and irrelevant contextual details. The researchers suggest that alternative training strategies may improve the probabilistic coherence of language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People increasingly use language models to support life decisions. Many such decisions involve a probabilistic forecast: How likely is a major life event, a natural disaster, or an economic outcome? Users of language models may implicitly trust that these forecasts fall out of a coherent world model. In this paper, we evaluate the coherence of language model probabilistic forecasts through a procedure that builds on a theorem due to de Finetti. We elicit forecasts from language models across events generated from stock returns data. We then use linear programs to compute the largest Dutch-book profit - the profit an arbitrageur could guarantee by betting against model-generated probabilities - which we use as a measure of incoherence. Our procedure does not require outcome labels, so we can evaluate coherence even in settings where outcomes are not observed or have not yet resolved. We find substantial evidence of incoherence in language model forecasts. Such incoherence increases when there are richer logical relationships between events, and irrelevant contextual details can increase incoherence by an order of magnitude. We conclude by discussing how alternative training strategies may improve probabilistic coherence.

items.title: Researchers develop Nemotron-3 models that surpass gold-medal thresholds in IOI coding competitions using post-training and feedback-driven refinement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-Training Language Models for Gold-Medal Performance in Coding Competitions
items.summary: Researchers present a specialization pipeline combining problem curation, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and a feedback-driven test-time strategy called GenCorrect to enhance large language models for competitive programming. Using 22,000 curated problems, they trained Nemotron-3-Nano-CC and Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC models, achieving scores exceeding gold-medal thresholds at IOI 2025 and 2026. The Ultra-CC system scored 535.4 out of 600 at IOI 2026 under human-like constraints, surpassing the top human contestant's score of 498.27. This marks the first AI system to outperform the highest-scoring human on an IOI problem set.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.02849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Competitive programming has become a key test of large language model reasoning, with international competitions such as IOI and ICPC representing its most challenging settings. We present an end-to-end specialization pipeline combining large-scale problem curation, synthetic reasoning traces, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL). Using 22,000 curated problems, we train Nemotron-3-Nano-CC (30B-A3B) with SFT and RL and Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC (550B-A55B) with SFT alone. We further introduce GenCorrect, a feedback-driven test-time compute strategy that iteratively generates, evaluates, and refines diverse solutions. On IOI 2025, Nano-CC improves from 130 points to 291 after post-training and to 468 with GenCorrect, exceeding the gold threshold of 438.3 while Ultra-CC reaches 502. Guided by these results, we develop a competition-specific Ultra-CC system and evaluate it prospectively during IOI 2026. Under the same time, internet-access, and submission constraints as human contestants, it scores 535.4 out of 600, exceeding both the gold threshold of 361.12 and the top human score of 498.27. To our knowledge, this is the first AI system to outscore the highest-scoring human contestant on an IOI problem set.

Using 22,000 curated problems, they trained Nemotron-3-Nano-CC and Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC models, achieving scores exceeding gold-medal thresholds at IOI 2025 and 2026. The Ultra-CC system scored 535.4 out of 600 at IOI 2026 under human-like constraints, surpassing the top human contestant's score of 498.27. This marks the first AI system to outperform the highest-scoring human on an IOI problem set.

items.title: Beyond Transfer Accuracy: Mechanism-Guided Controlled Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Transfer Accuracy: Mechanism-Guided Controlled Adaptation for Low-Resource Languages
items.summary: arXiv:2601.08146v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing circuit discovery methods rely on templated tasks with clean counterfactuals, limiting their use on diverse natural text. We adapt Contextual Decomposition for Transformers (CD-T) for unstructured settings via label-balanced activation means and task-directional relevance scoring, enabling counterfactual-free circuit discovery. We leverage the discovered circuits for Circuit-Targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (CT-SFT), restricting parameter updates to task-relevant heads and LayerNorm. Experiments on NusaX cross-lingual sentiment transfer show that CT-SFT is highly competitive for low-resource adaptation. While non-circuit sparse updates and full fine-tuning sometimes match target accuracy through capacity recruitment, CT-SFT most consistently avoids catastrophic forgetting, preserving source-language and related-task performance. Extensions to XNLI support the source-retention and intervention findings on a harder task and two model families, showing that circuit-targeted adaptation provides a more controlled, intervention-supported alternative to global fine-tuning.

items.title: ICE: Intervention-Consistent Explanation Evaluation with Statistical Grounding for LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ICE: Intervention-Consistent Explanation Evaluation with Statistical Grounding for LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2603.18579v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating whether explanations faithfully reflect a model's reasoning remains an open problem. Existing benchmarks use single interventions without statistical testing, making it impossible to distinguish genuine faithfulness from chance-level performance. We show that faithfulness is not a fixed property but an operator-dependent quantity that changes with the intervention method used to measure it. We introduce ICE (Intervention-Consistent Explanation), a framework that evaluates explanations against random baselines of equal size under multiple operators. Evaluating 7 LLMs across 4 tasks with deletion and retrieval infill operators, we find that switching operators crosses the positive-evidence threshold in 18% of configurations (5 of 28 attention comparisons), with gaps reaching 44 percentage points. Randomized baselines detect anti-faithfulness (explanations worse than random) in nearly one-third of English deletion configurations, invisible without random comparisons. These patterns persist across 6 non-English languages and 2 attribution methods. The methodology generalizes to step-level chain-of-thought evaluation, where preliminary results on 3 frontier models suggest that high accuracy does not imply faithful reasoning.

items.title: Agentic Scaffolding Amplifies Sycophantic Behavior in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic Scaffolding Amplifies Sycophantic Behavior in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2608.21377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models, the tendency to prioritize user agreement over truthful responses, has been documented extensively but studied primarily in single-turn settings. This paper investigates a critical question: does subjecting LLMs to greater interaction scaffolding make sycophancy better or worse? Across 4,800 veracity judgments (200 statements $\times$ 6 models $\times$ 4 conditions), we find that the interaction scaffolding characteristic of agentic systems (feedback loops, reconsideration checkpoints, and iterative refinement) systematically amplifies sycophantic behavior. Multi-turn interaction, user pressure, and iterative self-refinement each provide additional opportunities for models to drift toward agreement, and this drift coincides with a mean accuracy drop of $-6.3$ percentage points, establishing the capitulation as harmful rather than corrective. More capable models show larger amplification effects, a troubling inversion of expectations. We introduce the concept of agentic sycophancy amplification (ASA) and two novel metrics: capitulation rate and sycophantic capitulation rate. Our results indicate that as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, sycophancy becomes compounding rather than merely persistent. Systems designed with human oversight loops may inadvertently create the conditions for this drift.

items.title: The Illusion of Replacement: Rethinking Specialized Machine Learning Models in the Foundation Model Era [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Illusion of Replacement: Rethinking Specialized Machine Learning Models in the Foundation Model Era
items.summary: arXiv:2608.28980v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can the specialized architectures that machine learning has traditionally built for structured data be replaced by language-based models? This question is examined through a review of 159 papers (2016--2026) across nine modalities, with predictive accuracy considered alongside structural representation and computation. A distinction is made between performing a task and preserving and computing the structure that makes the task tractable, and existing approaches are organized into eight representational regimes, ranging from language-only systems to fully specialized architectures. Language-mediated models are found to be highly competitive in specific settings, including extreme few-shot prediction, discretized symbolic tasks, textually annotated knowledge graphs, and large-scale single-modality pretraining. However, whenever structural representation or computation is directly evaluated rather than accuracy alone, no evidence of general architectural replacement is found. Instead, a recurring pattern is observed across independent research communities: when language alone is insufficient, the missing structure is reintroduced through a graph module, structural tokens, specialized attention, or another non-linguistic component. In this sense, specialization more often relocates than disappears. Moreover, although performance of language-based models is improved by scaling, whether the gap to a structure-aware architecture can eventually be eliminated remains untested. The official repository for this work is available at https://github.com/kiyan-rezaee/language-vs-structure.

items.title: Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Diffusion Models are Associative Memories Capable of Retrieving Unseen Data
items.summary: arXiv:2604.26841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When do language diffusion models memorize their training data, and how to quantitatively assess their true generative regime? We address these questions by showing that Uniform-based Discrete Diffusion Models (UDDMs) fundamentally behave as Associative Memories (AMs) $\textit{with emergent creative capabilities}$. The core idea of an AM is to reliably recover stored data points as $\textit{memories}$ by establishing distinct basins of attraction around them. Historically, models like Hopfield networks use an explicit energy function to guarantee these stable attractors. We broaden this perspective by leveraging the observation that energy is not strictly necessary, as basins of attraction can also be formed via conditional likelihood maximization. By evaluating token recovery of $\textit{training}$ and $\textit{test}$ examples, we identify in UDDMs a sharp memorization-to-generalization transition governed by the size of the training dataset: as it increases, basins around training examples shrink and basins around unseen test examples expand, until both later converge to the same level. Crucially, we can detect this transition using only the conditional entropy of predicted token sequences: memorization is characterized by vanishing conditional entropy, while in the generalization regime the conditional entropy of most tokens remains finite. Thus, conditional entropy offers a practical probe for the memorization-to-generalization transition in deployed models.

items.title: SABER-Math: Automated Benchmark for Information Retrieval Evaluation in Mathematics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SABER-Math: Automated Benchmark for Information Retrieval Evaluation in Mathematics
items.summary: arXiv:2606.29894v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As agentic AI systems tackle more complex mathematical tasks, they increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) to search problem databases, theorem libraries, and educational resources. However, choosing the right retriever remains difficult, as it is infeasible to directly isolate its effect on downstream performance. On the other hand, existing retrieval-specific benchmarks often fail to capture fine-grained mathematical relevance, penalizing relevant documents. We address this gap by introducing SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical IR without expert annotation. Starting from 283K high-school-level math problems with solutions, SABER-Math builds challenging reranking tasks in three steps: (i) first, LLMs extract concise solution summaries and mathematical topics for each problem; (ii) then, per-query relevant documents are discovered using ontology topic-based and lexical solutions-summary-based similarities, and (iii) finally, a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament produces fine-grained relevance ratings for the documents. We evaluate lexical retrievers, specialized mathematical retrieval systems, and recent embedding models. We find that while modern embedding models substantially outperform classical and math-specific baselines, even the strongest systems struggle in symbol-heavy domains like Algebra and Calculus. Importantly, we show that general-purpose IR benchmarks such as MTEB do not reliably predict mathematical performance, especially for recent embedding models, highlighting the need for math-specific retrieval benchmarks.

However, choosing the right retriever remains difficult, as it is infeasible to directly isolate its effect on downstream performance. On the other hand, existing retrieval-specific benchmarks often fail to capture fine-grained mathematical relevance, penalizing relevant documents. We address this gap by introducing SABER-Math, the first fully automated benchmark for evaluating mathematical IR without expert annotation. Starting from 283K high-school-level math problems with solutions, SABER-Math builds challenging reranking tasks in three steps: (i) first, LLMs extract concise solution summaries and mathematical topics for each problem; (ii) then, per-query relevant documents are discovered using ontology topic-based and lexical solutions-summary-based similarities, and (iii) finally, a Swiss-style LLM preference tournament produces fine-grained relevance ratings for the documents. We evaluate lexical retrievers, specialized mathematical retrieval systems, and recent embedding models. We find that while modern embedding models substantially outperform classical and math-specific baselines, even the strongest systems struggle in symbol-heavy domains like Algebra and Calculus. Importantly, we show that general-purpose IR benchmarks such as MTEB do not reliably predict mathematical performance, especially for recent embedding models, highlighting the need for math-specific retrieval benchmarks.

items.title: Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy: Learning Autonomous Policies from Imperfect VLM Teachers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy: Learning Autonomous Policies from Imperfect VLM Teachers
items.summary: arXiv:2609.01567v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide useful priors for interactive decision-making, but using them directly as policies is expensive and brittle: they must be queried at every step, do not improve from environment interaction, and can repeat systematic errors. We study how to learn a cheap autonomous policy from an online, expensive, and imperfect but informative VLM teacher. We propose SAGE (Selective Agent Guidance via Entropy), a framework that queries a VLM only when the learner is uncertain, executes the suggested action during training, and distills guidance into a lightweight Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy. Because VLM advice is not always reliable, SAGE can weight teacher-action distillation using environment-derived advantages rather than treating all suggestions as equally useful. Across sparse-reward visual reasoning and navigation tasks, SAGE learns policies that act without VLM guidance at evaluation time and improves over unguided RL in several environments, including settings where the learned policy exceeds its VLM teacher. The results show that selective guidance is most beneficial when the VLM can help the agent discover high-reward trajectories, and less useful when unguided exploration already succeeds or teacher actions do not lead to informative experience. SAGE also reduces VLM usage by prompting the teacher only on a fraction of training steps and requiring no VLM calls at deployment. Overall, our results suggest that VLMs don't need to be used as fixed policies to be useful; they can instead act as temporary, imperfect sources of guidance whose value is tested and internalized through interaction.

items.title: PRO-Step: Step-level Process Reward Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PRO-Step: Step-level Process Reward Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2609.01658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation enhances Large Language Models by grounding responses in external knowledge, but multi-hop reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, where early retrieval failures confound subsequent steps. Standard outcome-based optimization only rewards the final answer, leaving intermediate retrieval and reasoning errors undetected. While existing process-based methods introduce step-level signals, they still score each step against the final answer, rewarding spurious successes where flawed retrieval coincidentally produces the correct answer. Step-level supervision in RAG requires evaluating both logical validity and evidential grounding at each step. We introduce PRO-STEP: we train a generative PRM that evaluates both dimensions, employ PRM-guided value tree search to construct preference pairs contrasting valid steps against flawed ones, and optimize the policy via step-level Direct Preference Optimization. Experiments on single and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that PRO-STEP achieves the best average EM and F1 across five benchmarks. Code, models, and training data are publicly available at https://github.com/keemminnke/PRO-Step.

items.title: VakyArth: Evaluating Pragmatic Competence in LLMs across Indic Languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VakyArth: Evaluating Pragmatic Competence in LLMs across Indic Languages
items.summary: arXiv:2609.01788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world communication often requires pragmatic reasoning: interpreting meanings implied through context and cultural convention rather than stated literally. Existing pragmatic evaluation remains largely limited to English and high-resource languages, leaving Indic languages unexplored despite their linguistic and cultural diversity. We introduce VakyArth, the first pragmatic benchmark for Indic languages, designed as a diagnostic evaluation covering Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. VakyArth evaluates models across five phenomena: deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence; through multiple-choice questions, natural language inference, and translation, with all items authored by native speakers. Across multilingual large language models (LLMs) of varying families and sizes, we find consistent failures on pragmatic meanings rooted in Indic linguistic and cultural conventions. Our analysis shows systematic differences across languages and tasks: MCQ accuracy exceeds NLI accuracy in all model-language combinations, translation performance does not reliably track pragmatic understanding, and Indo-Aryan languages show a translation advantage over Dravidian languages. We further show that automatic translation metrics can miss fluent but pragmatically unfaithful outputs, especially for implicature and deixis.

items.title: Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.01867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A major question in cognitive modeling concerns the behavioral alignment between large language models and humans across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks. Unlike standard LLMs, large reasoning models (LRMs) are optimized with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, encouraging correct solutions to reasoning tasks rather than preference-aligned responses. Recent work (de Varda et al., 2025) investigates the cost of thinking in humans and LRMs by comparing human reaction times with model reasoning traces across a range of reasoning tasks. We isolate this alignment by turning to abductive reasoning: unlike deductive tasks, its difficulty cannot be inferred from formal structure and offers no shortcuts a model could exploit to mimic effort without genuine search, providing firmer ground for empirical claims of shared effort. We find further evidence of alignment between LRM and human reasoning effort, as well as evidence that models and humans tend to make similar errors. Finally, we show that decoding methods that let models explore multiple reasoning paths increase alignment in reasoning cost between humans and LRMs across the three models tested.

Recent work (de Varda et al., 2025) investigates the cost of thinking in humans and LRMs by comparing human reaction times with model reasoning traces across a range of reasoning tasks. We isolate this alignment by turning to abductive reasoning: unlike deductive tasks, its difficulty cannot be inferred from formal structure and offers no shortcuts a model could exploit to mimic effort without genuine search, providing firmer ground for empirical claims of shared effort. We find further evidence of alignment between LRM and human reasoning effort, as well as evidence that models and humans tend to make similar errors. Finally, we show that decoding methods that let models explore multiple reasoning paths increase alignment in reasoning cost between humans and LRMs across the three models tested.

items.title: IDEEA: training-free Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: IDEEA: training-free Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching
items.summary: arXiv:2609.02089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steering aligns large language models (LLMs) by injecting a bias into selected activations at inference time, offering a far cheaper alternative to weight-update methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. However, most existing training-free steering methods are input-independent: a single direction is fitted once and shared across all inputs. This is fundamentally limiting as different inputs occupy different regions of the activation space and admit different optimal steering directions toward the same target concept, much as the gradient with respect to a fixed loss varies from input to input. We close this gap with IDEEA (Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching), a training-free framework for input-dependent steering. IDEEA clusters the positive and negative activation supports per attention head, and solves an optimal-matching problem to construct a set of cluster-conditional directions, all about the target concept. At inference time, it picks from this pool of directions and uses the one that best matches the input's own activation for steering. IDEEA aligns the model toward the target concept while preserving the input's original representation, evidence that activations encoding a concept occupy several distinct sub-regions of the representation space rather than a single one. IDEEA improves the truth $\times$ info rate in TruthfulQA by an average of 9.9% (up to 23.5%) over the best input-independent baseline.

items.title: Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2609.02108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to the auto-regressive paradigm. With bidirectional attention and any-order generation, DLMs naturally fit infilling tasks, which require generating a middle span conditioned on both the prefix and the suffix. However, infilling is sensitive to the length of the span, while DLMs require the length to be fixed before generation. Although prior studies extend DLMs to dynamic lengths, they still suffer from two limitations. (i) Sensitivity to initial length. These methods require a preset length to initialize the search and are highly sensitive to this initial length, often yielding suboptimal results. (ii) Inference inefficiency. They either insert length-changing operations during generation or repeatedly search for an appropriate length using multi-step denoising confidence, both of which introduce substantial extra forward passes and computational cost. Therefore, we propose PILL (Probing-based InfiLling with preset-Length-free decoding), an efficient infilling method for DLMs that requires no preset initial length and adds far fewer extra forward passes than baselines, substantially reducing inference time. Experiments show that, across five DLMs spanning different families, architectures, and training recipes on eight infilling benchmarks, PILL improves over the strongest baseline by +4.8 average pass rate on code and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text, while running 1.82x faster than that baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsu1023/PILL.
